newsitem.title: UK: Russia Eurobond spread steady in the grey market.
newsitem.headline: Russia Eurobond spread steady in the grey market.

text.p: The spread on Russia's $1.0 billion five-year Eurobond was stable in the primary or grey market on Friday, just below the 345 basis point launch spread over five-year U.S. Treasury notes, dealers said.
They said an imminent pay date was preventing large swings in the spread. The bond's pay date comes less than one week after launch, whereas most Eurobonds have a pay date about a month after launch.

The pay date -- when the money comes due to Russia -- is November 27, and the Eurobond will then enter the secondary market. Thereafter, the bond will become less liquid as investors will be holding the actual paper and it will not be as easy to obtain.
"It was a tactic to inhibit profit-taking," a dealer said, adding the banks in the syndicate did not want to be lumped with loose bonds that may have been sold back to them.
Russia's Eurobond was priced on Thursday to yield 345 basis points more than five-year U.S. Treasury notes.
The paper pays a coupon of 9.25 percent.

The bond was quoted at 343/342 bid/offer basis points more than the five-year U.S. Treasuries in the grey market at 1110 GMT on Friday. Traders said it was quoted at 345 basis points over on the brokers' screen.
At 1130 GMT the yield on the five-year Treasury was quoted at 5.94 percent.

"They've held the reoffer spread. To all intents and purposes the spread remains unchanged. The small fluctuations are fine tuning...in the context of a $1.0 billion issue, it is not really significant," a syndicate manager said.

Joint lead managers J.P. Morgan and SBC Warburg held the bulk of the paper at $800 million. The rest was being held with the six co-lead and 10 co-managers. Traders said the two leads could control the price and therefore volatility in the spread.
The spread tighted to test 330 b.p. in the first five minutes after the Eurobond was freed to trade on Thursday, but traded back to launch levels by the close of trade, dealers said.
"If you're talking about a World Bank or an EIB deal which is coming at 10 b.p. over, then a one basis point move is significant, but from 345 to 344 is much less significant," a trader said.

One analyst said uncertainty about whether the International Monetary Fund would pay out a delayed tranche of its $10 billion loan to Russia was preventing the spread from tightening further. Another said if there was any more nervousness about president Boris Yeltsin's health, the spread would widen.
But others said these concerns had already been factored into the price.
The Eurobond is the country's first international bond offering since the 1917 revolution and was heavily oversubscribed, syndicate officials said.
The investment banks said 44 percent of the issue was placed with investors in the U.S., 30 percent was sold into Asia and 26 percent in Europe, to both institutions and retail investors.
